sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

The terminal is the text-based interface to your computer — and nearly every tool in this course (Claude Code, Git, Node.js, Python) runs here. By the end of this lesson you'll have PowerShell open, understand exactly what you're looking at, and be able to navigate your file system, create folders, and run basic commands confidently. You'll also know the productivity shortcuts that make terminal work fast.

## What Is a Terminal?

When you use Windows normally, you're using a **GUI** (Graphical User Interface) — folders you can see and click, buttons, icons, windows. This is the interface designed for everyday users.

The **terminal** (also called the command line or shell) is a **text interface** to the same computer. Instead of clicking a folder to open it, you type `cd Documents` and press Enter. Instead of right-clicking to create a folder, you type `mkdir my-folder`.

**Why would anyone use this instead of clicking?**
- **Access:** Some tools only work from the terminal — Claude Code, Git, Node.js, Python all require it
- **Speed:** Once you know a command, it's faster than navigating menus (especially for developers)
- **Automation:** You can chain 50 commands together and run them all at once
- **Precision:** Commands are exact, reproducible, and scriptable; clicking is not
- **Remote work:** Servers don't have GUIs — anyone who manages servers uses the terminal

For this course, you'll use the terminal to run tools. You don't need to become an expert — you need to not be scared of a blinking cursor.

## The Windows Terminal Options

Windows has several terminal programs. Here's what each is and which to use:

**PowerShell** — The modern, recommended terminal for Windows. Built by Microsoft, it's powerful, well-documented, and handles both Windows-specific commands and many Unix-style commands (like `ls`, `pwd`, `mkdir`). **This is what we use throughout this course.**

**Command Prompt (cmd.exe)** — The older legacy terminal from the 1980s. It works for basic tasks but lacks modern features. If you see tutorials using it, the commands are slightly different. You don't need it.

**Windows Terminal** — A modern *host app* that can run PowerShell, Command Prompt, or other shells in a tabbed interface. If you have it (Windows 11 ships with it), great — use it. It runs PowerShell by default.

**Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)** — A full Linux environment running inside Windows. Useful for advanced development but not needed for this course.

**The answer:** Use PowerShell. When a tutorial says "open the terminal", open PowerShell.

## How to Open PowerShell

Learn all three methods — different situations call for different ones:

**Method 1 — Win + X menu (fastest):**
Press `Windows key + X`. A menu appears in the lower-left corner. Click:
- **"Terminal"** (Windows 11) — opens Windows Terminal with PowerShell
- **"Windows PowerShell"** (Windows 10) — opens PowerShell directly

**Method 2 — Start menu search:**
1. Press the Windows key
2. Type `powershell`
3. Click **"Windows PowerShell"** in the results

To open as Administrator (sometimes needed for installing tools): right-click the result → "Run as administrator"

**Method 3 — Right-click a folder (most useful for coding):**
In File Explorer, hold `Shift` and right-click any folder. Look for:
- **"Open in Terminal"** (Windows 11)
- **"Open PowerShell window here"** (Windows 10)

This opens PowerShell *already pointing at that folder* — the most useful method when you want to work inside a specific project directory.

**Method 4 — VS Code integrated terminal:**
In VS Code, press `Ctrl+\`` (backtick) or go to Terminal → New Terminal. This opens PowerShell inside VS Code, pointed at your current project. You'll use this throughout Parts 5–7 — it keeps your terminal and code in the same window.

## Reading the Prompt

When PowerShell opens, you'll see:

```
PS C:\Users\Alice>
```

Breaking this down:
- **`PS`** — PowerShell identifier (Command Prompt would just show `C:\Users\Alice>`)
- **`C:\Users\Alice`** — your current location in the file system
- **`>`** — the prompt character: PowerShell is ready and waiting

The current directory updates as you move around. It always tells you exactly where you are.

**If you see just `C:\Users\Alice>` without `PS`, you've opened Command Prompt instead.** Close it and open PowerShell.

**If you see `PS C:\WINDOWS\system32>`, you opened PowerShell as Administrator** and it defaulted to the system folder. Type `cd ~` to go to your home directory.

## Essential Commands

These 10 commands cover 90% of what you'll do in the terminal for this course:

**Navigation:**
```powershell
pwd                     # Print working directory — where am I?
cd Documents            # Change into the Documents folder
cd ..                   # Go up one level (to parent folder)
cd \                    # Go to the root of the drive (C:\)
cd ~                    # Go to your home directory (C:\Users\YourName)
cd C:\Projects\myapp    # Navigate using a full absolute path
```

**Listing files:**
```powershell
ls                      # List files and folders (short form)
dir                     # Same as ls (Windows-style)
ls -la                  # List including hidden files, with details
Get-ChildItem           # The full PowerShell command ls is short for
```

**Creating and managing:**
```powershell
mkdir my-project        # Create a new folder called my-project
new-item file.txt       # Create a new empty file
cp source.txt dest.txt  # Copy a file
mv old.txt new.txt      # Rename or move a file
rm file.txt             # Delete a file (permanent — no Recycle Bin!)
rm -Recurse folder      # Delete a folder and all its contents
```

**Viewing file contents:**
```powershell
cat filename.txt        # Print the contents of a file
Get-Content file.txt    # Same — full PowerShell command
```

**Running programs:**
```powershell
node --version          # Check if Node.js is installed
python --version        # Check if Python is installed
git --version           # Check if Git is installed
npm install             # Install Node packages
claude                  # Launch Claude Code
```

**Getting help:**
```powershell
Get-Help cd             # PowerShell help for the cd command
Get-Help mkdir          # Help for mkdir
code .                  # Open current folder in VS Code
```

## Productivity Shortcuts

These shortcuts make terminal work significantly faster:

**Tab completion — the most important habit to build:**
Instead of typing out a full folder name, type the first few letters and press **Tab**. PowerShell completes the name automatically. If multiple matches exist, keep pressing Tab to cycle through them.

```
cd Doc[Tab]    →    cd Documents
cd C:\Pro[Tab]  →   cd C:\Projects
```

Always use Tab completion. It prevents typos and speeds up navigation dramatically.

**Command history:**
- Press **↑ (up arrow)** to cycle through previous commands — no retyping
- Press **↓ (down arrow)** to go forward through history
- Press **Ctrl+R** and type a keyword to search history

**Other shortcuts:**
- **Ctrl+C** — Cancel a running command (stops it immediately)
- **Ctrl+L** — Clear the terminal screen (or type `clear`)
- **Home/End** — Jump to start/end of the current line
- **Ctrl+A** — Select all in the current line
- **Right-click** — Paste (in most PowerShell windows)

**Path tricks:**
- Drag a file or folder from File Explorer into the PowerShell window — it pastes the full path
- Type `code .` in any folder to open that folder in VS Code

**`rm` in the terminal is permanent.** Unlike deleting a file in File Explorer (which moves it to the Recycle Bin), `rm file.txt` in PowerShell deletes the file immediately with no undo. Triple-check before running any `rm` command — especially `rm -Recurse folder` which deletes everything inside a folder. When in doubt, use File Explorer to delete files while you're learning.

**On colour:** PowerShell windows can be blue, black, or any colour depending on your Windows version and settings. The colour is irrelevant — the `PS` prefix identifies PowerShell. Some companies have custom PowerShell themes that look different — the commands are the same regardless of appearance.

sections.title: Terminal Navigation & File Operations
sections.content:
Run every command below. Don't skip — the muscle memory from typing matters as much as the concept.

**Part 1 — Orientation**

**Step 1 — Open PowerShell:**
Use Win+X → Terminal (or Windows PowerShell). You should see `PS C:\Users\YourName>`.

**Step 2 — Confirm where you are:**
```powershell
pwd
```
You should see your user folder path.

**Step 3 — List what's here:**
```powershell
ls
```
You'll see your Documents, Desktop, Downloads, etc.

**Part 2 — Navigation**

**Step 4 — Navigate using cd:**
```powershell
cd Documents
pwd
```
Confirm you're now inside Documents.

**Step 5 — Navigate to your course folder:**
```powershell
cd ai-course-projects
pwd
ls
```
(If the folder doesn't exist yet, create it first: `cd ..` to go back, then `mkdir ai-course-projects`, then `cd ai-course-projects`)

**Step 6 — Practice going up:**
```powershell
cd ..
pwd
cd ..
pwd
```
You should be back at C:\Users\YourName after two `cd ..` commands.

**Step 7 — Navigate home directly:**
```powershell
cd ~
pwd
```
`~` is shorthand for your home directory — always works regardless of where you are.

**Part 3 — File and folder operations**

**Step 8 — Navigate to your course folder:**
```powershell
cd ~\Documents\ai-course-projects
```

**Step 9 — Create a subfolder:**
```powershell
mkdir terminal-practice
cd terminal-practice
pwd
```

**Step 10 — Create a file:**
```powershell
new-item hello.txt
ls
```
You should see `hello.txt` in the listing.

**Step 11 — View file contents (it's empty):**
```powershell
cat hello.txt
```
No output — the file is empty. That's correct.

**Part 4 — Tab completion and history**

**Step 12 — Use Tab completion:**
Back at `C:\Users\YourName`, type:
```
cd Doc
```
Then press **Tab** (don't press Enter yet). PowerShell should complete it to `cd Documents`. Press Enter.

**Step 13 — Use history:**
Press **↑ (up arrow)** several times to scroll through your recent commands. Find the `pwd` command and press Enter to run it again.

**Part 5 — Open VS Code from terminal**

**Step 14 — Navigate to your course folder and open VS Code:**
```powershell
cd ~\Documents\ai-course-projects
code .
```
VS Code should open with `ai-course-projects` as the project folder.

**What you've practiced:** navigating with cd, listing with ls, creating with mkdir/new-item, reading with cat, using Tab completion and history, and opening VS Code from the terminal. These cover everything you'll need for the rest of the course.

sections.question: You're in `C:\Users\Alice\Documents\ai-course-projects\exercises` and you want to get to `C:\Users\Alice\Documents\notes`. What is the most efficient command?
sections.explanation:
From `exercises` you need to go up one level to `ai-course-projects` (cd ..) and then into `notes` — so `cd ..
otes` is the relative path. `cd C:\Users\Alice\Documents
otes` also works but is longer (absolute path). `cd ..\..
otes` would go up two levels to `Documents` then look for `notes` there — wrong if `notes` is inside `ai-course-projects`. `cd notes` would only work if `notes` were a subfolder of `exercises`. Understanding relative paths like `..
otes` saves significant typing in everyday terminal use.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 4-3.** You can open PowerShell four different ways, navigate your file system with cd, list and create files, and use Tab completion and history to work efficiently. The terminal is no longer a mystery — it's a faster way to do what File Explorer does, plus access to all the tools that don't have GUIs.
